title: Broccoli and Alfalfa Sprouting Seed Recalls Are Active Right Now — What It Means If You Grow Sprouts on a Windowsill
intro: Windowsill sprouting is one of the few ways to grow real food in an apartment with zero grow light and zero floor space, which is exactly why it's worth pausing on this week's news: the FDA has multiple active recalls on sprouting seed tied to a Salmonella outbreak traced to a grower called Evergreen Fresh Sprouts, and at least one unrelated alfalfa sprouting seed recall for Salmonella and E. coli is also live. If you've got a jar of seed on the counter right now, it's worth two minutes to check it against the actual recall before you sprout anything else.

sections.heading: Check your seed bag against these exact recalls before you sprout anything this week
sections.body: Gardeners Basics recalled its Waltham 29 Broccoli Sprouting Seeds on October 8, 2026 — specifically the 1-lb white-and-green resealable pouch, UPC 848137042889, marked 'Packed for 2027,' from bulk lot #W4105 after the seed supplier found Salmonella in a sample. It was sold online only: Amazon, the company's own site, TikTok Shop, Walmart, eBay, and Etsy. Eden Brothers (calabrese broccoli seed) and EAK Distribution's Home Grown green sprouting broccoli seed were recalled the same week from the same contaminated supplier lot. Separately, Todd's Seeds LLC (Cookeville, TN) recalled 37,481 units of alfalfa sprouting seed for possible Salmonella and E. coli, sold through Amazon and direct-to-consumer, with Dec. 31, 2029 printed expiration dates. None of these are a 'maybe stop using it' situation — the FDA guidance is explicit: don't eat the seed or anything you've already sprouted from it, and don't compost it either, since that doesn't reliably kill the bacteria. Seal it in a bag and put it in household trash, then contact the seller for a refund.

products.name: Heavy-duty resealable freezer bags
products.blurb: What the recall notices actually tell you to use for disposal — seal the recalled seed (and any sprouts already grown from it) before it goes in household trash, rather than leaving an open bag of contaminated seed in a kitchen cabinet.
products.priceNote: A few dollars for a box; you only need one or two bags for this.

sections.heading: Sprouting is a genuinely higher-risk food category even without a recall
sections.body: The reason sprout seed shows up in outbreaks more than most produce isn't bad luck — it's the growing method. Sprouts germinate in warm, consistently moist conditions for several days, which is also the ideal environment for any bacteria already on the seed coat to multiply, and California's Department of Public Health has flagged the seed itself as the most likely contamination source in most sprout-related outbreaks. A tray or open jar that doesn't drain and rinse completely leaves standing moisture between rinses, which is exactly the condition that lets contamination take hold. A proper sprouting jar with a stainless mesh lid — rinsed and fully drained twice a day, jar tilted at an angle so no water pools at the bottom — is a meaningfully better setup than a bowl or a damp paper towel method for an apartment counter.

products.name: Wide-mouth mason jar sprouting kit with stainless mesh lid
products.blurb: Fits a standard wide-mouth mason jar; the mesh lid lets you rinse and fully drain without transferring seeds to a strainer, which is the step people skip when sprouting in a bowl.
products.priceNote: Inexpensive — usually sold as a 2-4 lid multi-pack that fits jars you likely already own.
products.searchQuery: sprouting jar kit stainless steel mesh lid wide mouth mason jar

sections.heading: Going forward, buy from a seller that actually publishes seed testing — not just a production date
sections.body: None of this week's recalled seed was mislabeled or sold by a shady seller — Amazon, Walmart, and TikTok Shop all carried it. The practical takeaway isn't to stop sprouting, it's to pick a supplier that tests for pathogens as a stated practice rather than one that doesn't mention it at all. True Leaf Market, for example, publishes that it voluntarily tests its sprouting seed lots for Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria (seed itself isn't FDA-regulated the way sprouts-for-sale are, so this testing is a choice, not a requirement) and retests for germination roughly every nine months. That's a self-reported practice, not an independent guarantee — it doesn't make a seed lot risk-free, and this week's recalls prove even established channels can carry contaminated stock. But a seller stating a testing process gives you something to point to, which a generic bulk-bin listing doesn't.

products.name: True Leaf Market organic sprouting seeds
products.blurb: A sprouting-seed brand that publishes its pathogen-testing practice (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria) rather than leaving seed safety unaddressed — look for the same disclosure from any brand before buying sprouting seed in bulk.
products.priceNote: Comparable in price to other sprouting seed brands; sold in small and bulk sizes.

conclusion: If you have broccoli or alfalfa sprouting seed in the apartment right now, check the brand and lot against this week's recalls before you touch it again — Gardeners Basics, Eden Brothers, Home Grown, and Todd's Seeds are the names to look for. Beyond this specific recall, sprouting's real risk is structural: warm, moist conditions for days at a time, which is why a proper rinse-and-drain jar setup and a seed supplier that's upfront about pathogen testing matter more here than in almost any other apartment-gardening category.
